articles.title: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama sold 1,500 mirrored balls for $2 each at Venice in 1966, decades later one of her paintings fetched $10.5 million
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 1966, visitors arriving at the Venice Biennale were confronted by an unusual sight. Spread across the lawn outside the Italian Pavilion were 1,500 .
articles.body: In 1966, visitors arriving at the Venice Biennale were confronted by an unusual sight. Spread across the lawn outside the Italian Pavilion were 1,500 shimmering silver spheres, each catching fragments of the surrounding architecture, the sky and anyone who stopped to look.Reportedly, among them stood Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, dressed in a gold kimono. She had not been formally invited to exhibit at the Biennale, yet she had found a way to put her work in front of its international audience. The installation was called Narcissus Garden, and Kusama did something even more unexpected with it. She began offering the mirrored balls to visitors for about $2 each.It was part artwork, part performance and part provocation aimed directly at the art market. Decades later, Kusama would become one of the world's most recognisable contemporary artists. Her polka dots, pumpkins and Infinity Mirror Rooms would turn her into a global cultural figure, while her paintings and sculptures began selling for millions.According to Reuters, her 1959 painting Untitled (Nets) eventually sold for $10.5 million at Phillips in New York in 2022, setting her auction record.Kusama turned 1,500 mirrored spheres into a giant field of reflectionsNarcissus Garden was not a conventional garden at all. Kusama arranged 1,500 mass-produced mirrored plastic spheres into a field of reflections outside the Italian Pavilion. Each polished surface returned a distorted image of the person standing nearby. Visitors could see themselves, the landscape and the surrounding buildings repeated across the installation. The title came from the ancient story of Narcissus, who became captivated by his own reflection. Kusama used that idea to turn the audience into part of the work. Instead of simply looking at a sculpture, visitors were repeatedly confronted with their own image.Kusama turned her Venice artwork into a $2-a-piece spectacleAs reported by Forbes, standing among the spheres in her gold kimono, Kusama invited visitors to buy them for 1,200 Italian lire, roughly $2 at the time.A sign associated with the installation described the sale as “Your Narcissism for Sale”, turning the mirrored objects into inexpensive pieces that visitors could actually take away. At a prestigious international art exhibition, Kusama was effectively saying that anyone could own a piece of the spectacle. Instead of allowing the work to remain something reserved for galleries, collectors or institutions, she broke it apart and offered individual spheres directly to the public.The act also questioned the way art acquires value. If a work displayed at one of the world's major exhibitions could be divided into hundreds of identical objects and sold cheaply, what exactly made one object 'art' and another merely a commodity?Kusama used 1,500 mirrored balls to claim her own space in VeniceKusama's position at Venice was unusual. She was not officially part of the exhibition, although sources note that she had support from Italian artist Lucio Fontana and permission from the Biennale committee's chairman to stage the installation outside the Italian Pavilion.The reality was more complicated. She was not an official exhibitor, but she did have support and permission to install the work. Her decision to turn the installation into a direct sale, however, was what created the controversy.The mirrored balls therefore did more than fill a patch of lawn. They gave Kusama a way to enter a major art event on her own terms. At the time, there was little indication that the artist would eventually become a household name.From $2 spheres to a $10.5 million auction recordThe original Narcissus Garden was made from plastic, but later versions used stainless steel spheres. The installation has since been recreated in different locations, allowing new audiences to encounter the same basic idea of a landscape transformed by hundreds or thousands of reflections.The work's longevity is partly down to its simplicity. A mirrored ball is not complicated. Put 1,500 of them together, however, and the effect becomes overwhelming. The viewer sees the environment multiplied across the surface of the installation, while their own reflection becomes impossible to ignore.Kusama's financial rise was far slower than the fame of her imagery might suggest. Her early career involved years of experimentation and periods in which her work was overshadowed by better-connected male artists. She moved to New York in 1957 and became involved in the city's avant-garde scene, developing the obsessive net paintings that would later become central to her reputation.One of those early paintings, Untitled (Nets) from 1959, eventually became her auction record and was on May 18, 2022, for $10.5 million.That figure is almost impossible to reconcile with the scene in Venice six decades earlier. There, Kusama was offering individual mirrored spheres for roughly $2. At auction, one of her paintings would later command millions.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Tourists carved names into around 350 bamboo stalks in Kyoto’s Arashiyama grove; the damage cannot be repaired, so officials began cutting bamboo and moving the grove beyond visitors’ reach
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Kyoto’s famous Arashiyama Bamboo Grove is facing growing damage from tourists carving names and other writing into its bamboo stalks. A city investiga.
articles.body: Kyoto’s famous Arashiyama Bamboo Grove is facing growing damage from tourists carving names and other writing into its bamboo stalks. A city investigation found that around 350 bamboo plants along the popular walking path had been damaged since spring 2025.The damage has prompted Kyoto city officials to take action. According to Strait Times, the city planned to cut down about 30 sq m of bamboo, including some of the damaged plants to protect the grove. Officials wanted to move the bamboo further away from the path so visitors cannot easily reach the stalks.The Arashiyama Bamboo Grove Path in Kyoto’s Ukyo ward is visited by both Japanese and international tourists. The trail runs through a bamboo forest and is known for its scenery. But writing and names carved into the bamboo have become an increasing problem as visitor numbers have risen again after the Covid-19 pandemic.The issue was highlighted during a city inspection last year. Officials found about 350 damaged bamboo plants along the path. When the area was visited on November 17, different types of writing could be seen carved into stalks on both sides of the busy trail. Some appeared to be names, including 'Kate' written in English and 'Yoshitaka' written in hiragana.Bamboo damage increased with visitor numbersThe Kyoto city government owns about 2.3 hectares of land along the path, where an estimated 7,000 bamboo plants grow naturally. The large number of damaged plants has raised concerns about the condition of the grove and its appearance.A 34-year-old company employee visiting the area with a friend from Kasugai in Aichi prefecture expressed disappointment after seeing the damage. “There’s graffiti everywhere, ruining the scenery,” she said.The problem is not limited to the appearance of the bamboo. According to the Kyoto Botanical Gardens, bamboo is unlikely to wither or fall because of surface damage. However, once a carving is made, it remains on the bamboo stalk.According to Kyoto prefectural police, the graffiti could constitute destruction of property. Local groups have also been trying to hide some of the damage. Associations in nearby areas, including a shopping district, have used green masking tape to cover carved sections of bamboo.Warning posters have also been placed on fences along the path and around 50 rickshaws. The notices are written in Japanese, English, Chinese and Korean.City plans special bamboo cutting Kyoto city officials and local residents held their first emergency countermeasures meeting on November 5 last year, to deal with the situation. The meeting led to a plan for a trial cutting of about 30 sq m of bamboo on city-owned land.The area will include bamboo that has already been damaged. Cutting bamboo is generally not allowed in the area, but the city plans to make an exception as a special preservation measure.The purpose was not simply to remove damaged plants. Officials wanted to push the bamboo groves further away from the walking path. This would create more distance between visitors and the stalks, making it harder for people to physically reach and carve them.Misao Hashimoto, chief of the city government’s scenic preservation division, said the bamboo forest belongs to the wider community and criticised the deliberate damage.“The bamboo forest is a shared property of the citizens. In particular, as the beautiful landscape of Arashiyama has been maintained through cooperation from the local community, it is extremely regrettable that it has been deliberately damaged,” Hashimoto said.In 2018 too, Kyoto city officials also installed fences after around 100 bamboo plants were defaced.The bamboo grove had seen less damage when visitor numbers dropped during the Covid-19 pandemic. However, concerned groups said graffiti became noticeably more common again as tourism increased after the pandemic.According to Alo Japan, Kyodo reported that the city and a local organisation has cut about 20 bamboo plants along both sides of the path to create enough distance so visitors could not reach the stalks. The plants were cut along aroughly 30-metre stretch. According to the report, only four of the bamboo plants that were removed had graffiti; some undamaged plants were also removed to create the required gap. The city said it would consider further removal after assessing the effect on the scenery.The wider Saga-Arashiyama area, where the bamboo path is located, is known for its scenery and has also appeared in many tanka poems. The area has been designated a special zone for the preservation of historic scenery under Japan’s Law on Special Measures concerning Preservation of Traditional Scenic Beauty in Ancient Capitals.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'It's your sense of entitlement': US officials slam Indian-origin entrepreneur Ankit Gupta over H-1B comments
articles.summary: US News: Indian-American entrepreneur Ankit Gupta landed in a soup after his H-1B comments on social media that stirred the hornet's nest, following which Gupt.
articles.body: Indian-American entrepreneur Ankit Gupta landed in a soup after his H-1B comments on social media that stirred the hornet's nest, following which Gupta made his X account private. Inspector General of the US Department of Labor took note of Gupta's comment and slammed him publicly, calling out what he termed as his "sense of entitlement". Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States Andrew Ferguson said individuals like Gupta do not have the best interests of Americans in their minds.Who is Ankit Gupta? What is the latest H-1B controversy?Gupta, a distinguished computer scientist from Harvard, is a serial entrepreneur and currently a partner of Y Combinator. Before joining YC, he was the co-founder and CTO of Reveries Labs. The controversy that he landed in stemmed from his comment on JD Vance's post."If an American corporation needs workers, it should hire and train Americans," Vice President JD Vance wrote on X, reacting to the Donald Trump administration's new H-1B visa fee. "in a win for the woke left DEI is back," Ankit Gupta commented, suggesting that if Americans have to be hired because they are Americans and not because of their skill, then it is DEI (Diversity, Equity and Inlcusion) only.The now-deleted post and the sarcasm did not go down well with America First commentators, and then it came to the notice of the DOL's Inspector General."Ankit Gupta thinks hiring Americans first—in America—is “DEI.” No, Ankit. It’s called putting your own citizens first. American companies. American jobs. American workers first. If that offends you, the problem isn’t America. It’s your sense of entitlement," D'Esposito said.As Gupta defended the H-1B hiring by Silicon Valley, he asked one commentator: 'what elements of H-1B immigrant culture do you not like? is it the willingness to work long hours? Or perhaps the education focus of their children?""Leaving trash everywhere, scamming people, endemic pathological dishonesty, atrocious aesthetic taste, need I go on," the commentator replied. "It's giving flyover country," Gupta wrote. Social media users started flagging this comment as a racist attack aimed at rural white Americans and asked YC to take action against Gupta."Hey @ycombinator this is a racist attack aimed at rural White Americans. Your policies mention that you do not tolerate any racism. It states that racial discrimination is a fireable offense. When can we expect you to fire Ankit Gupta?" one wrote.White House official reacts, YC CEO issues statementChairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States Andrew Ferguson, responded to the controversy and called YCombinator "a front for the far left"."Y Combinator is a supposed champion of “Little Tech” but perhaps they’re nothing more than a front for the far left. I’m deeply uncomfortable with wealthy investors attacking American workers like this. I’m afraid it’s increasingly obvious to many people that individuals such as this guy do not have the best interests of America and her citizens in mind," Ferguson wrote, referring to Gupta."The purpose of the American economy is to promote the general welfare of American workers, not provide jobs for the rest of the world," he said.Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan issued a statement saying that YC supports hiring and funding Americans.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Daniel Janzen: The ecologist who turned 169,000 hectares of Costa Rica into a giant forest filled with biodiversity
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Daniel H. Janzen is a biologist whose career has blurred the traditional boundaries between field ecology, evolutionary science and conservation. For .
articles.body: Daniel H. Janzen is a biologist whose career has blurred the traditional boundaries between field ecology, evolutionary science and conservation. For decades, his work has centred on tropical ecosystems, particularly the forests of Costa Rica, where he studied the intricate relationships between plants, insects and other organisms. His research eventually developed into something much larger than documenting species. Alongside biologist Winnie Hallwachs, Janzen helped shape the Área de Conservación Guanacaste (ACG), a vast conservation landscape in north-western Costa Rica that connects forests, volcanic ecosystems and marine environments. His work has also explored how conservation can function alongside local communities rather than treating protected areas as places completely separated from society. The University of Pennsylvania identifies Janzen as a leading figure in conservation biology, while his research has produced hundreds of scientific publications and influenced modern approaches to tropical biodiversity. His career demonstrates how understanding an ecosystem can become the first step towards protecting it for generations.How Daniel Janzen became fascinated by tropical ecosystems and field biologyJanzen's relationship with tropical biology began when he was young. According to the University of Pennsylvania and a biographical account published by the National Academy of Sciences, his interest in the tropics developed during a butterfly-collecting trip to Mexico when he was 14. He later studied biology at the University of Minnesota before earning his PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. His research became particularly focused on the relationships between tropical plants and animals. Insects, especially caterpillars and their interactions with host plants and parasites, became an important part of his scientific work. Since the late 1970s, Janzen and Hallwachs have carried out extensive field observations in Costa Rica's Área de Conservación Guanacaste. Their long-term work has helped document the complexity of tropical ecosystems rather than treating species as isolated components.Why Costa Rica became central to Daniel Janzen’s conservation workJanzen's role changed significantly during the 1980s, when scientific research began evolving into a much broader conservation effort. After being asked to examine environmental damage in Costa Rica, he became increasingly concerned that simply creating protected areas would not necessarily guarantee their survival. His focus shifted towards finding ways for conservation areas to function as part of the surrounding society. This philosophy became closely associated with the Área de Conservación Guanacaste. Janzen and Hallwachs helped develop the landscape into a large-scale conservation experiment involving restoration, biodiversity research, local employment and partnerships. A 2020 paper by Janzen and Hallwachs describes the ACG as a government-NGO conservation entity spanning roughly 169,000 hectares and incorporating ecosystems extending from the Pacific Ocean through dry forests and volcanic landscapes towards wetter forests. The approach challenged the idea that successful conservation simply means keeping people outside protected areas. Instead, Janzen argued for integrating biodiversity protection with the communities and institutions surrounding it.From cataloguing species to building a long-term biodiversity legacyOne of Janzen's most influential contributions has been his emphasis on understanding biodiversity at an enormous scale. The ACG has become both a conservation landscape and a long-term scientific research site, where species can be documented while their relationships with ecosystems are studied over decades. Janzen's work has also contributed to the development of DNA barcoding as a tool for identifying species. The University of Costa Rica notes that he helped promote the use of genetic “barcodes” to recognise species through molecular techniques, while his broader scientific output includes more than 500 publications. The scale of the ACG reflects the ambition behind this approach. Janzen and Hallwachs have described the area as a long-term effort to restore and conserve a connected tropical landscape while integrating it into Costa Rican society. For Janzen, therefore, conservation is not simply about preserving a snapshot of nature. It is about understanding how an ecosystem works, documenting its biological wealth and creating the social and scientific structures needed to keep that diversity alive far into the future.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In a plan hatched at Mark Zuckerberg's Hawaii compound in January, Meta explored laying off 60% employees, deleting layers of middle management and running product development with…
articles.summary: Tech News News: Meta explored cutting some of its teams by as much as 60 per cent and handing their work to AI agents, according to a Reuters special report on the co.
articles.body: Meta explored cutting some of its teams by as much as 60 per cent and handing their work to AI agents, according to a Reuters special report on the company's 2026 restructuring. The plan, code-named Project OT for Organization Transformation, imagined an AI-native Meta in which software did much of the daily work at the Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp parent, with a small core of high performers left to supervise it. What Meta actually got was 8,000 layoffs in May, a workforce in revolt, and a second round of job cuts cancelled at the last minute.Project OT came out of Mark Zuckerberg's January leadership retreat at his Hawaii compound and was built to run in two waves, one in May and one in November. Only the first landed. On the night of May 19, hours before the Meta layoffs began, Zuckerberg called off planning for the November wave, Reuters reported, citing internal documents and more than 20 people familiar with the company's inner workings. Meta went ahead the next morning and cut 8,000 jobs, roughly 10 per cent of its 78,000 staff. Meta has confirmed Project OT existed and acknowledged the 60 per cent scenarios, while saying it never intended to cut 60 per cent of the whole company.Mark Zuckerberg’s Project OT was designed to delete Meta's org chart, not just trim headcountThe structural half of the plan was the more radical one. Internal Meta posts described replacing traditional product teams of 10 to 20 specialists with pods of three to five people, everyone carrying the same generic title of builder. Layers of middle management would go. Unit heads would each oversee 30 to 50 employees, while pod leads ran daily work without formal authority. Meta's HR team also built a tool to identify irreplaceable talent, reviving the old Silicon Valley belief in the engineer who does the work of ten. By June, at least 11 units had adopted the pod structure.Meta's employee tracking programme for AI training is what tipped staff into revoltThe AI surveillance broke it first. In April, Meta told US employees their keystrokes, mouse clicks and screens would be captured so its AI models could learn how people complete real tasks on a computer. Chief technology officer Andrew Bosworth told staff there was no opt-out on a corporate laptop. More than 1,000 Meta employees signed a petition against the tracking. Flyers went up in offices and bathrooms, and staff replied to executive posts with pictures of elephants. Meta's internal Pulse survey registered the damage, with favourable sentiment falling from 74 per cent to 55 per cent. Engineers reassigned to a new Applied AI Engineering unit, writing coding puzzles as AI training data, described the work as rote.Meta's own AI productivity data never justified the AI restructuringThen the numbers turned. Bosworth posted in early June that code changes to Meta's internal platforms were up 220 per cent year on year, while changes that shipped a new or improved feature to users rose only 36 per cent. Infrastructure teams had flagged reliability warnings as early as March, and an April post described AI agents taking large, disruptive actions humans would not attempt. Major technical and security incidents climbed 40 per cent and firefighting time rose 70 per cent, per internal posts seen by Reuters. In June, attackers exploited Meta's new AI support bot to reach high-profile Instagram accounts, including the dormant Obama White House page.At a July town hall, Zuckerberg conceded AI agent technology had not accelerated as fast as he expected and asked for three to six more months. Meta has since paused the tracking, improved the office snacks and run a campaign about betting on people. It is also still committing at least $130 billion, about Rs 11.4 lakh crore, to AI infrastructure this year. And his assurance of no further layoffs arrived with two qualifiers attached: company-wide, and this year.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Spanish baby started making abstract drawings at 5 months, had paintings sold in Marbella and set a Guinness record at 10 months
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At five months old, John Christian Caldeira Weibull was already making pictures, although nobody could have known where those first marks would lead. .
articles.body: At five months old, John Christian Caldeira Weibull was already making pictures, although nobody could have known where those first marks would lead. Given an LED drawing tablet by his parents in Spain, the baby began moving across its surface and producing colourful abstract patterns. What might easily have been dismissed as a passing childhood curiosity became a regular activity, with John continuing to create new drawings as he grew. Within months, his work had moved beyond the tablet and into the physical world of exhibitions.On 19 October 2024, some of his paintings were displayed in Marbella, where several were sold. By then, John was still less than a year old. At 10 months and seven days, he also received a Guinness World Records title as the youngest male artist, making his unusually early start in art officially recognised.John's artistic journey started with a simple tabletJohn's introduction to drawing was remarkably simple. At five months old, he was given an LED drawing tablet by his mother and father. There was no formal training involved and, at that age, there could hardly have been any deliberate artistic technique in the usual sense.He began making marks anyway. The drawings developed into abstract compositions as John continued using the tablet. For his parents, watching their baby create these shapes was enough to keep encouraging him. What began as an ordinary object placed in front of a curious infant gradually produced a collection of drawings that could be kept and displayed.The early work also gave the family something tangible to look back on. Rather than treating the drawings as nothing more than a baby's pastime, they recognised that John's repeated interest in making them was unusual.His baby drawings were soon displayed in MarbellaThe move from a drawing tablet to physical artwork gave John's work a different setting. His abstract pieces could be presented as paintings rather than simply viewed as marks made during play.That distinction became important when one of his works was shown publicly in Marbella, Spain. On 19 October 2024, John's artwork appeared at an art exhibition there, where several of his paintings were sold.It was an unexpected progression for someone who had only recently started experimenting with a drawing surface. The exhibition also meant that the work was no longer confined to the family home. Other people were able to see the pieces, and some chose to buy them.For a child only months old, the circumstances were unusual, but the timeline remained straightforward: a drawing tablet at five months, a growing body of abstract work and then a public exhibition before his first birthday.John set a Guinness record before his first birthdayJohn's record arrived when he was just 10 months and seven days old. Guinness World Records recognised him as the youngest artist (male).The timing is what makes the record particularly striking. He had not spent years developing a conventional artistic practice before receiving the title. His creative activity had begun only months earlier, when his parents first placed the LED tablet in his hands.By then, however, there was a documented progression from those first experiments to artwork that had been exhibited and sold. The Guinness recognition placed his early drawings into a very different category, giving an official record to an activity that had started as an experiment at home.John's paintings went on sale while he was still an infantThe exhibition in Marbella took place on 19 October 2024, giving John's work a public platform while he was still an infant. Paintings were sold during the exhibition, adding a commercial element to an artistic practice that had begun with a baby simply making marks on a tablet.There is little need to attach an elaborate explanation to the drawings. They are abstract works, and their origin is unusual enough on its own. John was not following lessons or reproducing established forms. His parents had provided the tablet, and he developed his own way of interacting with it.The sequence of events is perhaps the most distinctive part of the story. John began drawing at five months. Several months later, his paintings had appeared at an exhibition in Marbella. At 10 months and seven days, he had a Guinness World Records title to his name.John's first artworks came before his first birthdayFor most children, making pictures becomes part of growing up and gradually changes as their ability to control a pencil, brush or other tool improves. John's story began much earlier, before those familiar stages of childhood drawing had even started.His first medium was an LED tablet rather than paper. His earliest pictures were abstract rather than recognisable scenes. And before he reached his first birthday, examples of his work had already been displayed in public.By 10 months and seven days, the Spanish baby had moved from making his first abstract drawings at home to holding a world record for the youngest male artist. It was a remarkably short journey from a glowing drawing screen to an entry in the Guinness World Records book.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: These are the fall 2026 fashion trends that will be everywhere next season, according to stylists and trend forecasters
articles.summary: From peplum knits to barn jackets and rich chocolate-brown suede, here's how to wear some of fall's biggest trends.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

As a style editor, I've learned that the best time to start planning a fall wardrobe is before everyone else does. This doesn't mean I buy all-new items on a quarterly basis — in fact, some cold-weather staples, like a solid pair of jeans and a good oversized sweater, will remain wardrobe staples season after season. My planning is pretty simple — I take inventory of what I like (and don't like) about my current wardrobe, keep an eye on emerging trends and decide which new pieces are worth adding.

I've worked at various publications and fashion brands for more than six years, and one of my favorite parts of the job is tracking runway shows, red carpets and social media to spot the next big trends. Based on what I've seen so far, many of the biggest fall 2026 fashion trends are nostalgic revivals or fresh takes on pieces you may already own. I also spoke with fashion experts and stylists about the styles they're most excited to wear this season and why they think these trends are poised to take off.

Once the weather cools down, it's time to start layering — and stylists recommend a classic trench for a polished look when temperatures dip. "Trench coats are a wardrobe staple that has continuously seen updates since last year," says trend forecaster Kendall Becker . While beige and tan are classic trench colors, Becker adds that navy and chocolate brown are also trending, along with leather and suede detailing.

Banana Republic Classic Men's Trench Coat

If you're looking to spice up a classic sweater this fall, there's a controversial 2010s trend that's making its way back into the spotlight — the peplum waistline. Even if you weren't a fan of the look 10 years ago, fashion expert and Afterpay and Cash App ambassador Zanna Roberts Rassi notes that the fall 2026 version of peplum feels less overwhelming and "much more refined." She adds, "Silhouettes are everything this season, and peplum hemlines are an easy way to define the waist and create a beautiful shape."

"It creates a really flattering shape while still feeling effortless and wearable," adds Blair Moore , founder and CEO of personal styling company Be Styled Co. "I'd pair a peplum cardigan or sweater with straight-leg or wider-leg denim and a simple flat or loafer."

Veatzaer Fall Puff Sleeve Peplum Sweater

Grace Karin Peplum Button Up Knit Sweater

Treasure & Bond Pointelle Peplum Sleeveless Sweater

"For those who have already found their favorite denim silhouette but still want a sense of newness, changing up the hue to a near-neutral is the perfect solution," says Becker. "Try a tonal look of shades of all greens or browns for this trend." You can treat olive, tan, brown and khaki as neutrals and pair them with most colors, according to Moore. She suggests pairing your earth-toned denim with a classic trench and loafers or a plaid blazer.

Old Navy High-Waisted Barrel Ankle Jeans

Lee Men's Extreme Motion Regular Straight Jean

Suede has been trending hard for the past few seasons and isn't going anywhere anytime soon. "A suede sneaker instantly reads more elevated than your standard pair," says Stacey Oliver , personal shopper and VIP stylist at Bloomingdale's. "The texture adds richness." Moore adds, "The key is choosing a low-profile silhouette rather than a chunky sneaker, which will look and feel more current and versatile."

According to Brendan Cannon , fashion stylist at Cannon Media Group, chocolate brown is having a moment — especially dark brown suede. "The hues of dark chocolate bring an instant sense of warmth and depth to cool-weather dressing," Cannon says. "Deep, espresso-hued suede is dominating over slouchy shoulder bags for fall 2026."

As for what colors to pair it with, Moore suggests "other rich fall colors like burgundy, olive green and cream." And don't worry about that old rule of not mixing brown and black: "That combination is one of the most modern things you can wear right now," says Moore.

articles.title: US Marines unveil new role for infantry in age of drones; how Indian Army is transforming
articles.summary: News News: The US Marine Corps is planning to redesign its infantry force for future wars dominated by drones, with a new roadmap calling for greater use of unma.
articles.body: The US Marine Corps is planning to redesign its infantry force for future wars dominated by drones, with a new roadmap calling for greater use of unmanned systems, counter-drone weapons, electronic warfare and precision fires at the small-unit level.The plan, called Ground Combat Element 2040, aims to make Marine ground units more capable of fighting on a battlefield saturated with enemy drones, sensors and surveillance systems.According to The War Zone (TWZ), the Marine Corps plans to push these capabilities down to the rifle-squad level. The approach would give small units their own counter-drone systems, drones and longer-range precision-strike capabilities, reducing their dependence on larger formations for some battlefield tasks.The Marine Corps' modernisation plan will be implemented in three overlapping phases. The first, covering 2026 to 2030, will focus on accelerating ongoing force-design reforms, addressing the immediate threat posed by drones and laying the groundwork for future investments.From 2031 to 2035, the Marines plan to expand the use of AI, autonomous systems and unmanned formations while strengthening layered counter-drone capabilities. By 2036-2040, the force is expected to move towards AI-enabled command and control, human-machine teaming and more dispersed, resilient formations with greater combat power at lower levels.The plan draws heavily on lessons from the Russia-Ukraine war, where drones have become a persistent threat to troops, armoured vehicles and other battlefield assets. Russian and Ukrainian forces are deploying large numbers of drones to create increasingly dangerous zones for ground troops, making protection against small unmanned systems a critical challenge for frontline units.The war in Ukraine has also demonstrated how rapidly drone technology is evolving, with newer systems increasingly capable of striking targets well beyond the immediate frontline. The experience is therefore forcing militaries to rethink not only how they use drones, but also how infantry units operate and survive while under near-constant surveillance and attack.What India is doing to build its drone-warfare capabilitiesThe lessons from Ukraine are not limited to the US. India, too, is moving to integrate drones more deeply into its ground forces, with the Army building unmanned capabilities across combat formations rather than keeping them confined to specialised units.In a June interview with TOI, then Army chief General Upendra Dwivedi said drones were being integrated into formations and sub-units, alongside counter-UAS and electronic-warfare capabilities.The Army is building a tiered drone structure. Ashni drone platoons are being introduced in infantry battalions for reconnaissance and offensive operations. It is also raising Shaktibaan regiments and Divyastra batteries as part of the broader push towards unmanned and precision capabilities, while work is underway on Shaurya squadrons for armoured formations.The focus is also on building a large pool of trained personnel. TOI reported that the Army plans to train around five lakh personnel in drone operations over five years, with about 50,000 already trained and a dedicated drone-warfare framework established across 19 military training establishments.At the same time, India is strengthening its counter-drone network with sensors, jammers, spoofers and kinetic systems, alongside electronic-warfare capabilities designed to detect, disrupt and neutralise hostile UAVs.The effort is now expanding into dedicated drone formations as well. The Army has raised its first Baaz Battalion under the Jalandhar-based 11 Corps. The unit is designed to operate larger UAVs, including Searcher, Heron and Hermes, and will serve as a centralised hub for flight operations, data exploitation, maintenance and coordination with troops on the ground.The battalion is also expected to use AI-based battlefield decision-support systems to process the huge volume of data generated by the Army's expanding drone fleet. The objective is to help commanders turn persistent aerial surveillance into actionable battlefield intelligence.

articles.title: Tropical Storm Dolly forms in the Atlantic. No, it wasn't named after Dolly Parton.
articles.summary: Tropical Storm Dolly has formed in the Atlantic, but its name has no connection to Dolly Parton. Heavy rain could reach parts of the Caribbean this weekend.
articles.body:
Tropical Storm Dolly formed in the central tropical Atlantic on Thursday morning, less than two days after country music queen Dolly Parton died. The storm's name is purely coincidental.

There are currently no coastal watches or warnings in effect, but National Hurricane Center forecasters advised people in the Leeward Islands to monitor the storm's progress.

"Little change in strength is forecast during the next 48 hours, and Dolly is forecast to degenerate into a tropical wave before it reaches the Leeward Islands," the NHC said in its latest advisory .

The storm names for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season are selected well in advance and are not chosen to honor specific people. The strict naming process is established by an international committee of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

Dolly is the fourth named storm of this year's Atlantic hurricane season.

According to the hurricane center's latest advisory, as of 11 a.m. ET on Thursday :

Dolly was located about 1,555 miles east of the Leeward Islands.

It had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph.

Starting late Saturday into Sunday, heavy rain from Dolly could begin affecting the Leeward Islands.

On Sunday and Monday, the Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and Hispaniola could also be affected by heavy rain.

It could produce flash flooding, especially in higher-elevation areas, the NHC said.

How are tropical cyclone names selected?

The WMO has developed different rules for naming tropical cyclones, depending on where they occur. Names are used to identify tropical cyclones because they've proven to be the fastest way to communicate warnings and raise public awareness of preparations. Naming storms also avoids confusion, especially when multiple storms are active.

For the Atlantic and Southern Hemisphere, cyclones are named alphabetically and alternate between men's and women's names.

These are the factors the WMO considers when selecting names:

Short names for ease of use in communication

Appropriate significance in different languages

Unique — same names cannot be used in other regions

How is the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season shaping up?

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season began on June 1 and lasts until Nov. 30. Forecasters with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration maintained their prediction for a below-normal season in the Atlantic basin, with seven to 13 total named storms expected, according to the Aug. 6 updated outlook. Of those named storms, two to six are forecast to become hurricanes, including up to two major hurricanes (considered Category 3, 4 or 5).

An average season has 14 named storms, including seven hurricanes, three of which are major.

The 2025 Atlantic hurricane season produced 13 named storms, including five hurricanes, four of which were major.

articles.title: American eagle vs Canadian goose: How a Goan photographer's US retreat was edited out
articles.summary: US News: TOI correspondent from Washington: The Trump White House thought it had found the perfect image to troll Canada: an American bald eagle, talons locked.
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: The Trump White House thought it had found the perfect image to troll Canada: an American bald eagle, talons locked around the neck of a Canadian goose, looking every inch like Uncle Sam had finally put the northern neighbor in a fatal headlock.There was just one problem. The goose eventually won the battle.The photograph, posted by the White House on social media amid the latest US-Canada trade spat, was meant to convey the unmistakable message that America was the eagle and Canada’s goose was cooked. Instead, the original footage, shot by a Goan immigrant, revealed an inconvenient director’s cut: after 20 minutes of aerial combat on ice, the Canadian goose fought back and the bald eagle eventually gave up and flew away.The spectacular encounter was shot on February 23, 2025, in Burlington, Ontario, by Mervyn Sequeira, who became an avid wildlife photographer after moving to Canada. Sequeira said he watched the bald eagle make repeated attacks on the goose. "At the end of 20 minutes, the bald eagle just gave up and took off," he told Global News, describing the encounter as "ballet on ice" -- although, he noted, it was hardly the nicest ballet because it was a life and death fight.Sequeira though resisted the temptation to turn his love of wildlife into foreign policy, saying he preferred to view it from “the naturalist point of view” rather than put a political spin on it. But the White House swooped in on the remarkable wildlife encounter, turning it into a diplomatic meme -- before it backfired.This has become something of a recurring problem for the MAGA flock: Its trolling does not always survive first contact with the internet. While the administration has embraced social media as a diplomatic weapon by using memes, photographs, maps and taunts to project primacy, its effort often has the polish of a high-school journal produced in the dorm after a night of wild partying.This week, for instance, the White House posted a map intended to promote Trump's proposal to call Lake Ontario “Lake America.” Unfortunately, Washington, DC, was misplaced, and several states were shuffled around like Monopoly pieces. The State Department suffered an even more spectacular cartographic failure a few weeks ago when a map of Africa at a major international conference mislabeled every country.There have been spelling and typographical gaffes, many from the President himself, whose claim of being a “stable genius” does not preclude clumsy errors like misspelling words like counsel and strait. In contrast to his witless trolling, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded with deadpan humor when a teleprompter malfunctioned at a recent news conference, joking that he did not regard it as a conspiracy -- a dig at Trump's earlier reaction to technical problems at the UN.Online jokesters have already generated goose bumps and hi-fives over the latest mishap, dubbing the photograph the “TACO eagle” — a reference to the long-running acronym “Trump Always Chickens Out.” Apparently, the bald eagle has just discovered Canadian diplomacy: talk tough, flap harder, fly home -- after cooking America’s gander.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Kishtwar forced abortion death: Three more held; total arrests now 5
articles.summary: India News: JAMMU: J&K Police have arrested three more suspects in connection with the death of a 14-year-old schoolgirl in Kishtwar district on Aug 20 follow.
articles.body: JAMMU: J&K Police have arrested three more suspects in connection with the death of a 14-year-old schoolgirl in Kishtwar district on Aug 20 following an alleged forced abortion bid, taking the total number of arrests in the case to five.Two key accused — the now-suspended schoolteacher who allegedly raped the minor several times, resulting in the pregnancy, and the teacher’s brother who aided the illegal abortion attempt — were arrested earlier. The latest arrests include a sweeper at Kishtwar district hospital and two others, SSP Naresh Singh said.Police have invoked charges under relevant sections of the Pocso Act, SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, and BNS against the accused in the FIR registered at Chatroo PS. The autopsy report confirmed the forced abortion bid and stated that the teen was five months pregnant, police said.A preliminary probe has so far revealed that the prime accused — who taught at the govt middle school where the minor studied — and his brother allegedly provided or administered medicines to the teen to terminate the pregnancy, the SSP said. After the girl’s health deteriorated, the duo took her to Chatroo PHC and later shifted her to Kishtwar district hospital, where she underwent an ultrasound examination, the SSP said.As her condition worsened, the teen was referred to Jammu GMC, over 200km away. Complications increased en route, and she passed away in an ambulance near Doda’s Batote. The death sparked massive outrage. articles.title: Donald Trump changes Lake Ontario’s name to ‘Lake America’ amid tensions with Canada
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump has ordered that Lake Ontario be referred to as “Lake America” in the United States, adding another point of tension to his .
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has ordered that Lake Ontario be referred to as “Lake America” in the United States, adding another point of tension to his increasingly strained relationship with Canada.Trump signed an executive order on Thursday changing the lake's name for the US geographic naming service. The decision applies to how the body of water is officially identified by US authorities, but Trump has no power to make Canada adopt the new name.The move follows Trump's earlier decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” for use by the US government.Trump signed the order at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. A map of the Great Lakes was displayed behind him, with the words “Lake America” written in large red letters over Lake Ontario.Speaking to reporters, Trump criticised Canada over trade and said, “They feel entitled and we can't have that,” while describing the country as “the worst” to deal with on trade.US-Canada trade tensionsThe announcement comes amid another escalation in the US-Canada trade dispute. The US recently announced 50 per cent tariffs on USD 20 billion worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries broke down.Trump has repeatedly criticised Canada since returning to the White House last year. He has also suggested that Canada should become the 51st US state, despite the two countries being long-standing allies.Why Lake Ontario mattersLake Ontario is one of the Great Lakes shared by the US and Canada. The international border runs through the lake, with New York State to its south and the Canadian province of Ontario to its north. The lake separates the US city of Buffalo from Toronto, Canada's largest city.Ontario is Canada's most populous province and is also the biggest export market for more than a dozen US states.The name Ontario has Indigenous origins. It comes from a word used by the Huron people, “oniatarí,” meaning “lake of shining waters”. The lake's name existed before European settlement, and the province later took its name from the body of water.There is no single international organisation with universal authority to decide the names of international bodies of water. The International Hydrographic Organization, whose members include the US and Canada, helps ensure that seas, oceans and navigable waters are surveyed and charted consistently and is responsible for naming some waterways.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: SRINAGAR: Congress Thursday turned down a proposal by National Conference (NC) to join the Omar Abdullah govt in J&K, saying the party would not deviate from its stand to stay away from the ministry until statehood was restored.“There is no doubt that NC is interested in seeing Congress join the cabinet. But Congress has taken a principled stand that until statehood is restored, it will not join the J&K govt. We have taken the usurpation of constitutional rights seriously. That’s why we have always maintained that Congress is an ally of the NC govt, but a cabinet berth is not acceptable to us until the constitutional right of J&K is restored,” J&K Congress president Tariq Hamid Karra said, adding, “With the Congress leadership at the highest level backing this position, we will not compromise on our principled stand.”Karra said Congress would continue to support and stand by the NC govt whenever it “feels threatened by BJP”, but that did not mean the party would not raise issues concerning the people, such as inflation and power tariff hike.The response came after deputy chief minister Surinder Choudhary said earlier in the day that NC was hopeful Congress would join the Omar govt and make it stronger. articles.title: Indians top nationalities working, settling in, visiting and getting citizenship in UK, but also top number of ‘voluntary returns’
articles.summary: Other News News: LONDON: Indians top the numbers of foreign nationals resettling in the UK, being granted British citizenship, gaining work visas, applying for study v.
articles.body: LONDON: Indians top the numbers of foreign nationals resettling in the UK, being granted British citizenship, gaining work visas, applying for study visas, and visiting the UK as a tourist, according to the latest immigration statistics released by the home office.In the year ending June 2026, Indians received the highest number of work visas at 47,009 (20% of total granted), of which 37,402 were worker visas (31% of those granted).The total number of work visas (234,841) was 18% fewer than the previous year due to policy changes and the abolition of the care worker visa and 62% fewer than the peak in the YE Dec 2023.Indians made the highest number of applications for study visas, applying for 89,763 visas. Of these, 83,958 were granted, the second-highest number after China. There were 383,455 study visas granted to all nationalities — 11% less than the previous year and 41% less than the peak in year ending June 2023.Chinese and Indian students accounted for 46% of sponsored study visas.Indians were the top nationality to visit the UK, with 514,398 visitor visas granted, making up 24% of all visitor visas and the largest nationality group granted settlement, with grants (35,384) increasing by 51% compared with the previous year. Indians also got the highest number of British citizenship grants at 24,851.Apart from legal routes, some Indians entered the UK illegally.A total of 471 Indians arrived on rubber dinghies from France, making Indians the 12th top nationality to enter this way, with the top five being from Eritrea, Sudan, Afghanistan, Somalia and Iran.Whilst Pakistanis were the top nationality to claim asylum, making 8,305 applications, of which 25% were granted at initial decision, Indians were the eighth top nationality to claim asylum, making 4,964 claims, of which just 30 (1%) were granted at initial decision. Apart from making an asylum claim after arriving on a small boat, 3,390 Indians made asylum claims after arriving in the UK on other visas.There are currently 2,224 Indian nationals living in taxpayer-funded asylum hotels and accommodation either waiting for an asylum claim or appealing one.There were 633 “enforced returns” of Indians (fourth highest) and 10,226 voluntary returns of Indians (largest nationality group) during this period.

articles.title: An Ohio couple spent 30 years scouring the country for pieces of an amusement park that closed in 1984; after donating the collection, an $11.5 million museum is being built to give it a permanent home
articles.summary: US News: Work on the outside of a new $11.5 million museum dedicated to preserving the history of the Idora Park amusement complex has been completed in downto.
articles.body: Work on the outside of a new $11.5 million museum dedicated to preserving the history of the Idora Park amusement complex has been completed in downtown Youngstown. The Mahoning Valley Historical Society (MVHS) said contractor Boak & Sons has finished replacing the roof of the four-storey building at 250 E. Federal St., along with major repairs to its windows and exterior masonry. The work clears the way for the next stage of the project, which will focus on designing the museum's interior. The building will eventually house tens of thousands of items collected over three decades by Canfield residents Jim and Toni Amey. The couple spent 30 years travelling across the United States to save rides, roller coaster cars, signs and other parts of the park. Idora Park closed permanently in 1984 after a major fire. In 2024, the Ameys formally gave their entire collection to the historical society, making it the foundation of the planned museum.As reported by Guy D'Astolfo for Business Journal Daily, MVHS bought the Federal Street building in 2023 for $1.9 million. Fundraising has so far brought in $4.04 million towards the overall project, including $1 million from the Ohio state capital budget and the Strategic Community Investment Fund. During a briefing at the building, Jim Amey reflected on how the project had grown from a personal hobby into a major regional effort. “It's overwhelming,” Jim said. “We never thought this would happen. We just started collecting trinkets at the beginning, and now this is a real sense of pride. This is big-time for us.” Toni Amey said that while their main collecting work has slowed, the couple still directs newly offered items to the historical society so that the collection stays together. “People are still contacting us,” Jim said. “We encourage them to donate it to the MVHS, but we will take it if they want us to.”Interior design phase beginsWith the roof and exterior work complete, Virginia-based design firm The Design Minds has been hired to plan the museum's interior through the rest of the year. The first and second floors in the eastern section of the building will contain the main public exhibition spaces. The third floor will be used for archive storage, while the fourth floor will continue to be occupied by existing commercial tenants. MVHS Executive Director Bill Lawson said designers are also collecting stories from people across the Mahoning Valley. These oral histories will help shape how the museum presents its collection. “They're talking to people in the community to learn what this place meant to them,” Lawson said. The building's exterior will also include features inspired by Idora Park. Plans include architectural details designed to resemble the shape of a roller coaster, as well as restored neon signs and original park structures. “We will want people to know what is going on inside here,” Lawson said. “It's a museum with a great deal of cultural experience, and we want them to see it.”Preserving Youngstown's cultural historyIdora Park opened in 1899 as an attraction connected to the local electric trolley system. For much of the 20th century, it became an important place for recreation among industrial workers and families across the Mahoning Valley. “Aside from the fun and recreation that went on here, there was great social and cultural significance,” Lawson said. “There was a dance hall, a convocation center, a ballroom and a baseball diamond. It was one of those places in the 20th century where people of diverse backgrounds who lived in their own enclaves came together. They walked down the midway and took it all in, and those are the stories that we're going to pull out.” The park's closure remains an emotional memory for many local residents. MVHS Board of Directors President Stacey Adger remembered seeing smoke rising from the park during the April 1984 fire that destroyed the famous Wildcat roller coaster and main arcade. “My family's visits usually centered around employee-family day,” Adger said. “Those were the days we usually got to go.” “Fast forward by 42 years and I'm pleased to be part of this exciting opportunity to share the love of this Youngstown treasure to future generations,” she added.State Representative Lauren McNally, who helped secure state funding with state Senator Michael Rulli, said the project could also support the downtown economy. “A big part of my job is advocating for organizations that make the Mahoning Valley a better place to live, and a project like this makes that job easy,” McNally said. “This renovation is more than just a beautiful building. It will be a place where the community gets to tell its story and invest in its future.” The historical society plans to begin interior construction once it reaches its remaining fundraising targets.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2020, Albany brought 1,500 feet of Patroon Creek back above ground after decades in a pipe; three of the next five years saw peak flows exceed the old pipe’s capacity
articles.summary: US News: In 2002, city engineers in Albany moved a 1,500-foot section of Patroon Creek into a large underground pipe, covering the urban stream to make room fo.
articles.body: In 2002, city engineers in Albany moved a 1,500-foot section of Patroon Creek into a large underground pipe, covering the urban stream to make room for nearby development. Eighteen years later, the city changed direction. In 2020, workers removed the culvert inside the 72-acre Tivoli Lake Preserve, bringing the stream back to the surface as part of a major "daylighting" project. The work was designed to restore the creek's natural flow, create more green space and improve flood protection for nearby communities. Water monitoring since the stream was uncovered shows how important the extra space has become. According to a success story published by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), flow data collected by the US Geological Survey (USGS) showed that peak flows at the site exceeded 500 cubic feet per second in three of the five years after the project was completed. Engineers had identified 500 cubic feet per second during early feasibility studies as the maximum amount of water the old underground pipe could carry before overflowing into nearby neighbourhoods. If the stream had remained inside the 2002 pipe during those heavy rain events, stormwater could have backed up into surrounding residential areas. Instead, the wider open channel and restored floodplain gave the water more room, allowing the surge to move safely through the preserve towards the Hudson River.Designing for extreme weatherThe daylighting project was carried out by the Albany Water Board in partnership with state environmental officials. City records show that construction was supported by a $1 million grant from the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) through Clean Water Act Section 319 funding. Instead of forcing large volumes of water through a narrow, smooth pipe, where water can move quickly towards downstream bottlenecks, engineers created a wide, winding earth channel. Native plants and rock structures were added to the channel to slow the water and reduce erosion along the banks. The design also allows Patroon Creek to spread into nearby restored wetlands during major storms. This gives the water space to slow down and soak into the ground rather than relying entirely on hard drainage infrastructure. The project also addressed a long-running water quality problem. In 2002, the same year the creek was placed underground, Patroon Creek was added to New York State's Clean Water Act Section 303(d) list of impaired waters because of very low dissolved oxygen levels. The underground pipe had separated the creek from the air and reduced natural aeration, creating poor conditions for aquatic life. Bringing the creek back into the open air and restoring natural movement over rocky sections has helped improve oxygen levels. The wider channel also helps filter urban runoff by trapping sediment and pollutants from roads before they reach Tivoli Lake.Environmental benefits for local communitiesThe restored stream runs through Tivoli Lake Preserve, next to the historic Arbor Hill and West Hill neighbourhoods. Both communities are officially recognised by state regulators as Environmental Justice communities. The EPA said bringing Patroon Creek back to the surface has provided important environmental and recreational benefits to residents who have historically faced pollution and industrial development. The stream is also becoming an important part of wider plans to improve outdoor recreation in the region. According to the Capital Area Regional Transportation Council, formerly known as CDTC, the Patroon Creek Greenway plan aims to connect the Albany waterfront along the Hudson River with the Albany Pine Bush Preserve. Including the restored section of Patroon Creek within Tivoli Lake Preserve has helped create a connected green corridor. The area provides walking routes, access to nature and opportunities for outdoor education for nearby residents. The decision to remove the underground pipe has also provided a direct benefit for flood protection.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
